questions.stem: Which of the following is true about an adjacency matrix?

options.text: It is always symmetric for undirected graphs.
It is always symmetric for directed graphs.
It has more rows than columns.
It cannot represent graphs with loops.

questions.explanation: In an undirected graph, the adjacency matrix is symmetric because the edge $(i, j)$ is the same as $(j, i)$. For directed graphs, this symmetry does not hold.

distractorRationale.b: Directed graphs do not necessarily have symmetric adjacency matrices.
distractorRationale.c: An adjacency matrix is square, having the same number of rows and columns.
distractorRationale.d: Adjacency matrices can represent graphs with loops by having non-zero diagonal entries.

questions.stem: A graph has 5 vertices and 8 edges. Using the handshake lemma, calculate the sum of the degrees of all vertices. Provide your answer as an integer.
questions.explanation: According to the handshake lemma, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is twice the number of edges. Therefore, $2 \times 8 = 16$.

questions.stem: What is an advantage of using an adjacency list over an adjacency matrix?

options.text: It uses less space for sparse graphs.
It is more efficient for dense graphs.
It is always faster to iterate over all edges.
It is easier to implement for directed graphs.

questions.explanation: Adjacency lists are more space-efficient for sparse graphs because they only store existing edges, unlike adjacency matrices, which allocate space for every possible edge.

distractorRationale.b: Adjacency matrices are more efficient for dense graphs because they allow constant-time access to check if an edge exists.
distractorRationale.c: Iterating over all edges is generally faster with adjacency matrices for dense graphs.
distractorRationale.d: Both adjacency lists and matrices can be implemented for directed graphs with similar ease.

questions.stem: Explain why the sum of the degrees of all vertices in a graph is twice the number of edges.
markingGuide: Each edge contributes to the degree of two vertices in an undirected graph.
The sum of degrees counts each edge twice, once for each vertex it connects.
This results in the sum being twice the number of edges.
questions.explanation: In an undirected graph, each edge $(u, v)$ contributes 1 to the degree of vertex $u$ and 1 to the degree of vertex $v$. Thus, every edge is counted twice in the sum of degrees, leading to the relation $\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|$.

questions.stem: In a directed graph, what does the out-degree of a vertex represent?

options.text: The number of edges directed towards the vertex.
The number of edges directed away from the vertex.
The total number of edges connected to the vertex.
The number of loops at the vertex.

questions.explanation: In a directed graph, the out-degree of a vertex is the number of edges that originate from that vertex, pointing to other vertices.

distractorRationale.a: This describes the in-degree, not the out-degree.
distractorRationale.c: This would be the degree in an undirected graph, not specifically the out-degree.
distractorRationale.d: Loops contribute to both in-degree and out-degree, but are not the sole component of out-degree.

questions.explanation: Vertex $A$ has outgoing edges to vertices $B$ and $C$. Therefore, the out-degree of vertex $A$ is 2.

questions.stem: Describe a scenario where an adjacency matrix is more beneficial than an adjacency list.
markingGuide: Dense graphs where most possible edges are present.
Fast edge existence checks are needed.
Graphs where constant-time access to edge information is crucial.
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix is beneficial in dense graphs because it allows for constant-time edge existence checks. This is useful when the graph has many edges, and quick access to edge information is required.

questions.stem: What does the diagonal of an adjacency matrix represent in a graph with loops?

options.text: The number of vertices in the graph.
The presence of loops at each vertex.
The total number of edges in the graph.

questions.explanation: In an adjacency matrix, a non-zero entry on the diagonal indicates a loop at that vertex, as it represents an edge from the vertex to itself.

distractorRationale.a: The diagonal does not represent the number of vertices.
distractorRationale.c: The diagonal does not directly indicate the total number of edges.
distractorRationale.d: The degree of a vertex is not solely determined by the diagonal.

questions.stem: Explain why adjacency lists are often preferred for representing large sparse graphs.
markingGuide: Space efficiency: only store existing edges.
Faster iteration over edges compared to adjacency matrices.
Reduced memory usage when the graph has few edges relative to vertices.
questions.explanation: Adjacency lists are preferred for large sparse graphs because they only store existing edges, making them more space-efficient. This reduces memory usage and allows for faster iteration over edges compared to adjacency matrices, which allocate space for all possible edges.
